FISHING METHOD / REDFISH

Sight fishing: what tailing redfish mean

Sight fishing means finding the fish before you cast. A tailing redfish feeds head-down in shallow water, with its tail above the surface. Look for that feeding posture, then plan your approach. The useful tide depends on the flat: a South Carolina flood-tide rule does not transfer to a Texas bay.[1] [2]

Quick answer

Sight fishing means finding the fish before you cast. A tailing redfish feeds head-down in shallow water, with its tail above the surface. Look for that feeding posture, then plan your approach. The useful tide depends on the flat: a South Carolina flood-tide rule does not transfer to a Texas bay.[1] [2]

01

What does tailing redfish mean?

The fish tips down to feed while its tail breaks the surface. TPWD describes this over shallow grass. A visible tail is a useful clue to the fish’s position; it does not promise that the fish will take your fly.

Pause before the cast. Locate the fish’s head and leave space for the fly or lure to reach it. Ask your guide to explain the approach before you start moving across the flat.[1]

02

When do redfish tail?

Use this table to separate habitat facts from local tide advice. “Not stated” means the linked source gives no threshold. It does not mean that the factor has no effect.[1] [2]

Swipe the table to compare all columns.

When redfish tail: two different flats settings
FactorTexas agency guidanceHilton Head and Beaufort guide
Tide stageNo single stage stated.High tides flood short spartina flats.
DepthShallow water; no tailing-depth threshold stated.About a foot of water over the flat is the guide’s starting point.
LightNot stated.Not stated.
BottomGrass; vegetated bay habitat.Short spartina grass or sand; avoid tall-grass wading routes.
03

Which tide should you use for a first trip?

Choose the place before you choose the tide. LoCo Fly Charters describes flooded flats around Hilton Head and Beaufort and identifies the Fort Pulaski station for its local planning. That station and those flats are not a tide prescription for another coast.

Ask your guide which station, flat and access window apply. Write down the time to leave as well as the time to arrive. A tide app gives a prediction; it does not show every small channel on your walking route.[2]

  • ✓Name the flat and the tide station.
  • ✓Agree on the approach and return route.
  • ✓Ask how wind changes the plan.
  • ✓Keep a boat-based alternative if wading does not suit the group.
04

How should you approach a sight-fishing trip?

Decide whether you want a skiff day or a wading day before you pack. Ask the guide how far you must walk, how long you may stand and how the return route works. Choose footwear for the confirmed bottom, not just the word “flats”.

TPWD lists shrimp, crab and baitfish fly patterns for red drum. Ask the guide to choose the size and weight for the day. Start with the tackle you own and check that it suits the boat and method.[1]

A few good questions

Before you head out

Is a tailing redfish feeding?

The term describes a redfish feeding head-down with its tail exposed above shallow water.

Do redfish always tail at high tide?

No universal tide rule is established here. The South Carolina guide describes flooded grass flats; choose the tide for the actual place.

Is sight fishing only fly fishing?

No. The method starts with locating a fish before the cast. Ask which fly or conventional outfit suits the planned trip.

Does a visible tail guarantee a bite?

No. Treat it as a clue to location and posture, not a promise of a catch.

Can a beginner take a sight-fishing trip?

Ask the guide about casting help, walking distance and time on your feet. Agree on the access method and practise the required cast before the outing.

Should you wade through tall marsh grass?

LoCo Fly Charters advises against it in its local flats guidance because of soft mud, deeper water and oysters. Use an agreed access route.
